summary: Specifies the algorithms, parameters, key formats and sizes, and signature formats used in BGPsec. It includes example UPDATE messages, private keys and certificates. It updates RFC 7935 and was replaced by RFC 8608.

eli5.summary: The list of exactly which locks and keys the route-signing system uses. It has since been replaced by RFC 8608.

subtitle: The cryptographic algorithms and key formats used to sign and verify BGP route announcements.

tldr.problem: BGPsec needs to sign and verify route announcements to prevent hijacking, but it must use algorithms that keep signatures small to avoid inflating BGP update messages. Standard RPKI algorithms are too large for route-level signing.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies ECDSA with the P-256 curve and SHA-256 hashing for BGPsec signatures, which produces smaller signatures than RSA while maintaining strong security. It defines the exact key formats, certificate request formats, and signature encodings.
tldr.outcome: BGP routers can now cryptographically verify route origins using standardized, compact signatures. RFC 8608 later updated these specifications.

today: RFC 8608 updated this specification with revised BGPsec algorithms and key formats.

sections.title: BGPsec and Cryptographic Signing
sections.content:
BGPsec is a set of security extensions for BGP that allow routers to cryptographically sign the route advertisements they propagate. This prevents an attacker from announcing routes they do not own or from modifying route announcements in transit. Each router in a chain of route announcements signs a message with its private key, and downstream routers verify the signature using the router's public key.

The challenge for BGPsec is scale. BGP update messages are already bandwidth-constrained, and adding signatures to every route announcement can quickly balloon message sizes. Regular RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) certificates use RSA signatures, which are large. BGPsec needs a more compact signature algorithm to keep update messages small while still providing strong cryptographic security.

This RFC specifies the algorithms, key sizes, and signature formats used by BGPsec. It also specifies how BGPsec routers request certificates from the RPKI hierarchy and defines the format of the signatures embedded in BGP UPDATE messages.
sections.eli5: Routers need to sign their route announcements ("I own 192.0.2.0") to prove they are not lying. But BGP messages are already crowded, so signatures must be small. This says which math to use for small, strong signatures.

sections.title: Signature and Hash Algorithms
sections.content:
BGPsec uses the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) on the P-256 curve for all signatures, paired with the SHA-256 hash function. The ECDSA signature on P-256 produces a 64-byte signature, which is significantly smaller than an RSA-2048 signature (256 bytes).

The combination of ECDSA with SHA-256 is identified by the OID ecdsa-with-SHA256. When a BGPsec router requests a certificate from the RPKI Certification Authority, it must use this algorithm suite in the PKCS#10 certificate request. The RPKI CA verifies the request signature using ECDSA-P256-SHA256.

This algorithm choice differs from the rest of the RPKI infrastructure, which predominantly uses RSA. The difference is justified by the need to minimize BGPsec update message sizes while maintaining equivalent cryptographic security.
sections.eli5: BGPsec uses ECDSA on the P-256 curve (a specific elliptic curve math problem) with SHA-256 hashing. This produces signatures that are much smaller than RSA but just as secure.

sections.title: Key Pair Formats and Sizes
sections.content:
BGPsec private keys are ECDSA keys on the P-256 curve. A P-256 private key is a single 256-bit integer (32 bytes). BGPsec routers generate these keys locally and keep them secure on the router hardware.

The public key is represented in uncompressed form, which means it is encoded as a single point on the P-256 elliptic curve: the X and Y coordinates, each 32 bytes. In certificates, the public key is placed in the subjectPublicKey field using the ECPoint encoding specified in RFC 5480. The algorithm identifier in the certificate MUST use the OID id-ecPublicKey with parameter secp256r1.

Private key format is left to local policy; BGPsec does not mandate how routers store or protect private keys (though hardware security modules are recommended for production deployments).
sections.eli5: BGPsec private keys are 32-byte numbers generated by each router. Public keys are two 32-byte numbers (the X and Y coordinates on the curve) that the router shares with the certificate authority.

sections.title: Signature Encoding in BGPsec UPDATE Messages
sections.content:
In BGPsec UPDATE messages, signatures appear in the Signature_Block list. Each signature is an ECDSA signature over the P-256 curve, which naturally produces two integers: r and s (each 256 bits). The signature is encoded as specified in RFC 3279 Section 2.2.3, which encodes both r and s in a fixed 64-byte format.

Each Signature_Block also includes an Algorithm Suite Identifier field, a single octet. For ECDSA with SHA-256, this identifier MUST be 0x1. The value 0x0 and 0xFF are reserved. This allows for future algorithm suites (like ECDSA with SHA-512) to be added without backward compatibility issues.

Certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists continue to use the standard RPKI signature format specified in RFC 7935, while only BGPsec UPDATE messages and certificate requests use the ECDSA signature format specified here.
sections.eli5: In BGP UPDATE messages, each signature is 64 bytes (the two parts of an ECDSA signature: r and s). The message also includes a one-byte identifier saying which algorithm was used (0x1 means ECDSA with SHA-256).

sections.title: Algorithm Suite Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains the BGPsec Algorithm Suite Registry. Currently, only one algorithm suite is registered: identifier 0x1 for ECDSA with SHA-256. The registry allocates identifiers in the range 0x2 through 0xEF for future algorithm suites via the Standards Action process.

Future algorithm suites might include ECDSA with different curves or hash functions. When a new suite is standardized, IANA will assign it an identifier that BGPsec routers can then reference in UPDATE messages, allowing for seamless algorithm agility without breaking existing deployments.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps a list of which one-byte numbers mean which algorithm. Right now 0x1 means ECDSA-P256-SHA256. If new algorithms are invented, they get new numbers.
